round 3 — Mechanism (prosemirror-view 1.42.3 dist/index.js:3904-3916, :2261-2264): Firefox focuses the editing host on a mousedown inside the contenteditable=false wrapper, and 20 ms later handlers.focus writes the editor's own selection into the DOM; stopEvent keeps ProseMirror's mousedown handler out on purpose (it would node-select the picture, a non-collapsed selection ProofDocument's click handler steps aside for), so for a reader who had not clicked into the text the caret went to the document's start and a long document scrolled away before the mouseup. Placing a collapsed caret just after the picture on mousedown makes that the selection ProseMirror restores. Chromium focuses the link itself, so the editor is unfocused when the caret moves and the DOM selection is untouched (editorOwnsSelection). preventDefault on mousedown was rejected: Firefox then starts no drag, and round 2's drag of the fallback link would be lost.

round 4 — Settled by documenting rather than changing: the fallback link shows two hover cards in the live editor (RefPreviewHost's on data-dispatch-href, and proof-sdk's link card on any a[href] in an editable view). Suppressing the library's card would need either dropping the real href (which the version view's click and a middle click use) or stopping mousemove propagation at the link (which would also hide the event from ProseMirror's document-level drag-selection tracking), so both cards stay and the passage says so; a one-card design is the architect's to file if wanted.

discoveredComplexity: Pre-existing, not changed here: a paragraph that ends in a picture is ~115 px tall in the editor whatever the picture's size, because ProseMirror's cursor hack after a contenteditable=false leaf (``) gets Tailwind preflight's `display: block` and Typography's `.prose img` 2em margins. Measured on the plain `` path too (`![logo](https://example.invalid/logo.png)` → 115.19 px), so it predates this change; the fix would be a `.milkdown img.ProseMirror-separator` rule in styles.css, a separate issue for the architect.
